newsitem.title: USA: CNS sees Breathe Right unhurt by Acutek.
newsitem.headline: CNS sees Breathe Right unhurt by Acutek.

text.p: CNS Inc said any patent suit by Acutek Adhesive Specialties Inc would be without merit and a recently reissued patent to which Acutek claims to have a license "has no effect on CNS' marketing plans or the patent protection for its Breathe Right nasal dilator."
Shares in CNS were up 1-5/8 at 15-1/2.

"While we have not yet been served with Acutek's lawsuit and are aware of the possibility of it only because of their press release, we believe that any such suit would have no merit and we would vigorously defend our position in court," said CNS chairman and chief executive Dr. Daniel Cohen.

"Clearly, the device described in the patent asserted by Acutek is significantly different from both the Breathe Right strip and the external nasal dilator that Acutek marketed in the United States prior to the issuance of the Breathe Right patent," Cohen said.

Several U.S. patents cover the basic invention of the Breathe Right and potential modifications of it, the company said, adding the patents provide significant protection for the product. Patent applications are pending in several countries overseas, it said.

"In July 1996, CNS brought suit against Acutek in U.S. District Court, alleging that Acutek had infringed its patents. The suit was settled on the basis of representations by Acutek that it had stopped manufacturing and selling the product. We believe that Acutek's external nasal dilator -- if ever again produced and marketed -- will infringe on the Breathe Right patents," Cohen said.
"CNS created and continues to define the external nasal dilator category, and we will be aggressive in defending our intellectual property rights," Cohen said.
An Acutek spokeswoman said the Inglewood, Calif.-based company was preparing a statement to respond to CNS.
